title: IoT · 03 · Wireless LANs
notes: PDF page numbers are used throughout. Version questions test technical mechanisms rather than potentially misleading headline maximum-rate tables.

Clarifications beyond the slides: an ordinary AP bridges at layer 2; it is not merely a physical-layer device. RTS, CTS and ACK are MAC control frames, not ARP payloads. Address 4 is used for four-address distribution-system forwarding, not ordinary ad-hoc traffic.

Timing questions use SIFS<PIFS<DIFS, not the slides' oversimplified claim that their durations are simply propagation-time multiples. RTS/CTS is optional, and stations hearing a relevant RTS reservation must not simply ignore it because they missed CTS.

802.11 version comparisons are scoped to the generations discussed in the deck, not a claim about the latest available standards. BSS/ESS architecture does not imply that every BSS must contain an AP.

questions.prompt: Distinguish wireless from mobile, and infrastructure from ad-hoc operation. Give one example showing why the distinctions are independent.
questions.answer: Wireless describes a radio link; mobile describes movement. Infrastructure uses an AP or base station; ad-hoc nodes communicate without one. A fixed Wi-Fi sensor is wireless but stationary, and an ad-hoc network need not have moving nodes.
questions.explanation: Radio medium, movement and network organization are separate properties.

questions.prompt: Compare single-hop infrastructure, multi-hop infrastructure and multi-hop ad-hoc networks. What changes about the path to the Internet?
questions.answer: Single-hop infrastructure reaches an AP directly. Multi-hop infrastructure uses wireless relays to reach infrastructure. Multi-hop ad-hoc nodes relay among themselves without requiring an AP or Internet gateway.
questions.explanation: The presence of multiple wireless hops does not by itself determine whether infrastructure exists.

questions.prompt: Explain path loss, interference and multipath, and give one reason an apparently nearby wireless receiver may still have a poor link.
questions.answer: Path loss reduces signal strength with propagation. Interference adds competing signals; multipath produces delayed copies via reflections. Obstacles, interferers or destructive multipath can make a nearby link unreliable.
questions.explanation: Distance alone does not characterize a wireless channel.
key_points: Delayed reflected copies and a valid consequence

questions.prompt: With a fixed received SNR, why might choosing the highest-rate modulation increase packet loss? Explain how a rate-adaptation policy should use SNR and a BER requirement.
questions.answer: Higher-order modulation packs more bits per symbol but can require higher SNR to distinguish symbols reliably. Choose the highest rate whose BER meets the requirement and lower it when channel quality falls.
questions.explanation: Raw data rate can rise while useful delivered throughput falls through retransmissions.

questions.prompt: Why can two senders that both reach an AP fail to sense each other? How does RTS/CTS help, and why does it not guarantee zero collisions?
questions.answer: Obstacles or attenuation can hide the senders from each other. The AP's CTS announces a reservation to nearby interferers. RTS frames can still collide and control frames can be lost, so protection only reduces risk.
questions.explanation: Sensing at a sender is not the same as interference conditions at the receiver.
key_points: Control collisions or losses remain possible

questions.prompt: Describe a BSS, an ESS and the distribution system. How does the AP connect the wireless segment to other devices?
questions.answer: A BSS is a basic service group; an infrastructure BSS includes an AP and associated stations. An ESS links BSSs through a distribution system. The AP bridges wireless frames to that system, commonly a wired LAN.
questions.explanation: Clarification: bridging is a data-link function, rather than just physical signal repetition.

questions.prompt: Assume independent bit errors with probability p. Derive the probability that an L-bit frame has at least one error. Why does this motivate fragmentation?
questions.answer: All bits are correct with probability (1-p)^L, so frame error probability is 1-(1-p)^L. Larger L raises the risk of a failed frame; smaller fragments limit the amount retransmitted after an error.
questions.explanation: Fragmentation improves error recovery at the cost of additional per-fragment overhead.

questions.prompt: For p=10^-5 and L=1500 bytes, estimate the frame error probability using independent errors. Explain why reporting p as the packet loss probability would be misleading.
questions.answer: L=12000 bits, so P_error=1-(1-10^-5)^12000, approximately 0.113 or 11.3%. A frame fails if any bit is wrong, so its error probability can greatly exceed the individual bit error probability.
questions.explanation: A small per-bit probability accumulates over a long frame.
key_points: Bit error differs from whole-frame failure

questions.prompt: Compare DCF with the optional PCF described in the deck. How can contention-based and contention-free service coexist in a BSS?
questions.answer: DCF uses distributed CSMA/CA contention. PCF has an AP-based coordinator poll stations during a contention-free period. The BSS can alternate contention periods and coordinator-controlled periods.
questions.explanation: PCF is optional and its scheduled period is not the same as ordinary DCF contention.

questions.prompt: Why might a WLAN use RTS/CTS for large frames but skip it for short ones? Distinguish reservation overhead from the cost of a failed data transmission.
questions.answer: RTS/CTS consumes airtime even when no collision would occur. For long data frames, preventing a collision or replacing it with a short RTS collision can save substantial airtime. For short frames the extra exchange may cost more than it saves.
questions.explanation: The threshold trades constant protection overhead against collision cost.
key_points: Short frames may not justify protection

questions.prompt: Explain the ordering SIFS<PIFS<DIFS. How does it prioritize an ACK and allow the point coordinator to begin PCF service before ordinary DCF traffic?
questions.answer: An immediate ACK waits SIFS; the coordinator can act after PIFS; new DCF contenders wait DIFS. Shorter waits gain access first when the channel becomes idle.
questions.explanation: The ordering establishes priority without requiring all stations to negotiate for each immediate response.

questions.prompt: Explain why WLAN slot time depends on the physical-layer implementation, and distinguish an interframe space from a contention backoff.
questions.answer: Slot time is a PHY-dependent timing unit for contention. An interframe space is a required idle interval associated with frame priority; backoff adds a random number of slots to spread competing attempts.
questions.explanation: A random backoff and a fixed priority wait serve different functions.

questions.prompt: Describe passive and active scanning and what association achieves. Does hearing a beacon already mean the station has an IP address?
questions.answer: Passive scanning listens for AP beacons; active scanning sends probe requests and receives responses. The station selects an AP and exchanges association messages. Link association and IP configuration are separate; DHCP may follow.
questions.explanation: Discovery, joining the link and obtaining network-layer configuration are distinct steps.
key_points: IP configuration is a separate step

questions.prompt: Two neighboring APs use nearby partially overlapping 2.4 GHz channels. Explain the interference risk and why choosing different channel numbers alone is insufficient.
questions.answer: A channel occupies a frequency range wider than the spacing between channel centers, so different numbered channels may overlap substantially. Planning should use suitably separated channels rather than merely unequal numbers.
questions.explanation: This tests spectral overlap without treating one region's channel availability as universal.

questions.prompt: Classify association, RTS, CTS, ACK and user-data frames. Distinguish the roles of CRC, ACK and sequence numbers.
questions.answer: Association is management; RTS, CTS and ACK are control; user payload travels in data frames. CRC detects corruption, ACK confirms reception, and sequence numbers support recognizing repeated frames.
questions.explanation: Error detection, confirmation and duplicate suppression solve different reliability problems.

questions.prompt: A station H sends a frame through AP P to a wired router R. What are Address 1, Address 2 and Address 3? Explain why two addresses would not be enough.
questions.answer: Address 1 is P, the immediate wireless receiver; Address 2 is H, the wireless transmitter; Address 3 is R, the ultimate link-layer destination across the distribution system. The AP must preserve both the radio-hop and bridged-endpoint information.
questions.explanation: The receiver of this radio transmission need not be the destination of the bridged payload.
key_points: Immediate receiver differs from ultimate destination

questions.prompt: A wired router R sends a packet to wireless station H through AP P. Give the Ethernet source/destination and the resulting Wi-Fi Address 1–3 values.
questions.answer: Ethernet source is R and destination is H. On the wireless hop Address 1 is H, Address 2 is P and Address 3 is R.
questions.explanation: The transmitting bridge changes while the original endpoint identity remains available.

questions.prompt: When would 802.11 need four addresses rather than the three used in ordinary infrastructure traffic? Name the four distinct roles.
questions.answer: Distribution-system forwarding over a wireless link can require immediate receiver, immediate transmitter, original destination and original source. Four-address frames preserve all four when both ends of the wireless hop are forwarding devices.
questions.explanation: Clarification: ordinary ad-hoc operation alone does not imply a fourth address.

questions.prompt: H roams between APs connected by bridges within one IP subnet. Why can its IP address and TCP connections remain valid? What changes if it must join a different subnet without a mobility mechanism?
questions.answer: Within one subnet, the radio association and forwarding path change while the IP endpoint stays the same. On a different subnet it generally needs different IP configuration, so existing TCP connections bound to the old address cannot simply continue.
questions.explanation: Link mobility and network-layer address continuity are separate concerns.
key_points: Address change disrupts ordinary TCP continuity

questions.prompt: A receiver accepts a frame but its ACK is lost. What does the sender do, and how do Retry, sequence number and fragment number help the receiver?
questions.answer: The sender may retransmit. Retry flags the retransmission, the sequence number associates it with the original frame, and the fragment number identifies the piece. Together they support duplicate detection while still acknowledging delivery.
questions.explanation: Correct reception followed by ACK loss must not produce duplicate user data.

questions.prompt: What problem do the Power Management and More Data flags address? Explain why a sleeping station may need the AP to buffer traffic.
questions.answer: A station indicates its power-saving state so the AP can accommodate periods when its receiver is unavailable. The AP buffers pending traffic; More Data indicates additional queued frames for that station.
questions.explanation: Reducing receiver-on time saves energy but requires coordination for downlink delivery.

questions.prompt: Compare Duration/NAV, the MAC CRC, the PHY preamble and the PHY header. Which one synchronizes reception and which one reserves airtime?
questions.answer: Duration advertises the exchange's remaining reservation for NAV. MAC CRC detects frame errors. The PHY preamble helps synchronization and detection; the PHY header communicates parameters needed to decode the transmission.
questions.explanation: These fields operate at different stages and should not be treated as interchangeable overhead.
key_points: Preamble synchronizes and PHY header describes transmission

questions.prompt: Compare 802.11b, 802.11a and 802.11g in terms of band and transmission technique. Why was g useful for compatibility with existing b deployments?
questions.answer: b uses the 2.4 GHz band and DSSS-family transmission; a uses 5 GHz and OFDM; g brings OFDM to 2.4 GHz while supporting coexistence/compatibility with b equipment.
questions.explanation: A generation's rate is only one dimension; frequency and compatible PHY behavior also matter.
key_points: g: 2.4 GHz OFDM with b compatibility

questions.prompt: What mechanisms let 802.11n and 802.11ac increase rates over earlier generations? Why does a wider channel or more antennas not automatically deliver the advertised maximum?
questions.answer: n uses multiple spatial streams and wider channels; ac extends channel width and stream count and uses denser modulation. Actual performance depends on device capabilities, channel quality, contention and protocol overhead.
questions.explanation: Headline PHY capacity differs from application throughput and requires suitable conditions.
key_points: Practical conditions and overhead limit throughput

questions.prompt: According to the mechanisms emphasized in the deck, how does 802.11ax extend ac? Give two changes and explain why increasing modulation order is conditional on channel quality.
questions.answer: The deck highlights operation in 2.4 and 5 GHz rather than ac's 5 GHz-only operation, uplink multi-user/multi-stream capabilities, and 1024-QAM. Denser constellations need adequate SNR to keep symbols distinguishable.
questions.explanation: This is a comparison of the covered generations, not a complete inventory of ax features.

questions.prompt: A WLAN shows a high negotiated PHY rate but poor application throughput. Give three distinct explanations from the deck and one useful observation for distinguishing each.
questions.answer: Interference or multipath can raise error/retry rates; contention can increase channel-busy time and backoff; short payloads or RTS/CTS can make overhead dominant. Compare retry/error statistics, busy airtime, and frame-size/control-frame distribution.
questions.explanation: A high PHY rate describes transmission while active, not how often useful data can be delivered.
key_points: PHY rate differs from delivered throughput
